newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM faces confusion on native land claims.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM faces confusion on native land claims.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard met state political leaders on Wednesday to discuss the confusion created by a court ruling bolstering Aboriginal land claims.
Next month, Howard will meet Aboriginal leaders, farmers and miners. He said compromises would be needed following the December ruling affecting pastoral leases.
Australia's High Court ruled last month that traditional Aboriginal ownership of land could co-exist with pastoral leases.

The surprise High Court decision -- known as the Wik case after a tribe of the Aboriginal litigants -- extended a 1992 High Court ruling that allowed Aboriginal people to claim native title to vacant state-owned land.
Pastoral leases are held by farmers and for grazing of sheep and cattle and cover about 40 percent of Australia's land area.
Many of Australia's far-flung gold and base metal mines are also on pastoral leases and miners have joined farmers and ranchers in objecting to the ruling.
The ruling overturned the position of the former Labor government -- under which the Native Title Act was passed in 1993 -- that pastoral leases extinguished native title.
"On the advice available to me at the present time, this decision has the potential to create enormous uncertainty," Howard told reporters after Wednesday's meeting.
"It's not an option to do nothing."
The Wik decision dealt with the right of Aboriginal people to hunt and hold tribal ceremonies on pastoral land if they can prove a traditional connection to that land.
Aboriginal groups argue it will have no economic impact, but farmers say the now ruling will sow uncertainty.
Howard said on Wednesday the ruling could mean a farmer might have to seek permission from a native title holder to build a dam on his property.
"It can't be left as it is," he said. "We have to try to get a solution that is reasonably acceptable to all the people involved."

Howard said he had not decided how to resolve the politically sensitive row. The government would do nothing to breach "the spirit of racial harmony", but he asserted the government's right to amend legislation if necessary.
Aboriginal groups, meanwhile, began a two-day meeting with miners and pastoral lease-holders at the northern Australian town of Cairns.
People of Aboriginal descent make up less than two percent of Australia's 18 million population.
